description: Is TF healthy, and what is slow. Provisioned from docker/observability/dashboards/ — edits made here cannot be saved back.

panels.description: Fixed TraceQL against Tempo. These are searches, not aggregates: each row is one trace, and opening it is the whole point of the row.
panels.title: Traces — what just happened

panels.description: One row per org's GitHub poll cycle. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall. Duration is the whole org's refresh + diff + emit; the waterfall says which repo batch spent it. An empty list means no org polled GitHub in the window — which for an org that tracks no repos is the correct answer, not a fault.
panels.title: GitHub poll cycles

panels.description: One row per org's Jira poll cycle. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall.
panels.title: Jira poll cycles

panels.description: One row per org's Linear poll cycle. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall. A cycle that stopped short says why in its `outcome` attribute: `unconfigured` (no Linear credential or workspace, or no rule in it), `no_armed_teams`, `disabled` (the source is turned off), `policy_unreadable` (the source's on/off setting could not be read, so the cycle skipped rather than poll), or `rate_limited`.
panels.title: Linear poll cycles

panels.description: One row per background job cycle, each for one org (`org.id`). `job` names the job: `scorer`, `profiler`, `reconciler`, `reach_refresher`, or `marketplace_aggregator`. `outcome` is set only where a job reports one. `wrote` and `no_write` say whether a reach refresh changed the mirror: most `no_write` rows are cycles that found nothing to do (a TTL skip), but an enumeration the refresher declined to write is one too. `nothing_to_score` is a scorer cycle that found nothing to do, `no_model` a scorer cycle skipped because the org has no background-jobs model, and `shutdown` a cycle cut off by a stop. A failed cycle has status `error`. `marketplace_aggregator` appears only when it recomputes; a cycle inside its TTL records nothing. Click a Span ID to open the cycle's trace; the filter icon keeps one job.
panels.title: System job cycles

panels.description: Every verb, not just reads — the mutating routes are where the slow work usually is (writes, delegation dispatch). Server spans are named "<METHOD> <route pattern>", never the concrete path, so no repo name or other tenant data reaches this list. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall. The DB spans underneath usually explain the time. Empty is the healthy state.
panels.title: API requests slower than 500 ms

panels.description: Every span that ended with an error status, any subsystem. Click a row to open that trace's waterfall. Anticipated skips (provider backoff, dedup, quiet-skip) are recorded as an `outcome` attribute rather than an error status, so this list stays things that are actually wrong.
panels.title: Errored spans

panels.description: Derived from the spans above by Tempo's metrics generator (traces_spanmetrics_*) and remote-written to Prometheus. Covers every instrumented subsystem at once, so it grows on its own as new span families land.
panels.title: RED — rate, errors, duration by span name

panels.description: Calls per second for every span name Tempo has seen. The legend is sorted by peak, so the busiest paths are at the top.
panels.title: Request rate by span name

panels.description: Share of calls that ended with an error status. Span names with no errors are absent rather than plotted at zero, so 'No data' here means nothing errored and anything drawn is worth a look.
panels.title: Error rate by span name

panels.description: Click an exemplar dot to open the trace behind that sample — the metrics→traces bridge, and the fastest route from 'the p95 moved' to the one request that moved it.
panels.title: p95 latency by span name

panels.description: Scraped from each pod's :9464. Every series here is per-process: in a scaled fleet the pods are separate lines, told apart by tf_service (control vs executor).
panels.title: Runtime — the pod itself

panels.description: Multi mode holds two pools per pod that behave nothing alike — `admin` serves the JWT-less background jobs, `app` serves RLS-bound request handlers. Local mode has one, named `local`. A max of 0 means unlimited.
panels.title: DB pool connections

panels.description: Time spent blocked waiting for a connection, per second of wall clock. This is the saturation signal the connection counts can't give you: a request waiting on the pool hasn't started a statement yet, so it looks exactly like a fast query until it shows up here. Flat zero is the healthy shape.
panels.title: DB pool contention

panels.description: TF's own server histogram, independent of the trace pipeline — this panel keeps working with tracing switched off. Routes are ServeMux patterns, so no concrete path (and no repo name) reaches the label.
panels.title: HTTP requests by response status

panels.description: A number that only ever climbs is the signature of a leaked goroutine — a poll cycle or run that starts one per iteration and never returns.
panels.title: Goroutines

panels.description: RSS as the kernel sees it. In multi mode the executor's dispatch admission gate is driven by host memory headroom, so this is the number that decides whether a run is allowed to start.
panels.title: Resident memory

panels.description: Empty unless a Slack app is connected. Sustained retries are the precursor to Slack disabling the app's event subscription, and app_rate_limited means Slack is dropping deliveries at the source — those are never retried.
panels.title: Slack ingest

panels.description: The router's spans. One `route.event` root per durable-queue row, linked back to the `event.enqueue` that produced it rather than parented to it — a poll cycle emits many events and they route later, possibly on another pod. The three routing panels all empty means nothing routed in the window, which for a deployment tracking no repos or projects is the correct answer, not a fault. The two panels under them are the router's queue workers, which run when a task frees or a score is written, not once per routed event.
panels.title: Event pipeline — what routing did with each event

panels.description: One row per queue row the router claimed, sorted by the wait rather than by recency. `queue.wait_ms` is the enqueue→claim interval — over before this span starts, so nothing else in the trace can show it, and without it a backed-up queue and slow routing look identical. `disposition` is what routing decided: most values end the pipeline early (`frozen`, the three `taskless_*`), so a pass that did nothing looks like a fast span until you read the column, and `error` is a disposition rather than a span error status — the store call that failed carries the status on its own span, where the cause is. Click a Span ID to open the routing trace; the filter icon keeps one disposition. Empty means nothing routed in the window.
panels.title: Routed events — queue wait and disposition

panels.description: `route.event` and `route.delegate` call rates, per minute. The delegation line is the operator-visible consequence of a trigger's configuration — enable a prompt_trigger and this is where it moves, and there is nowhere else it shows. The `conversation.id` each delegation started is an attribute on the `route.delegate` span, reached by opening that event's trace. A flat zero delegation line under a live routing line is the ordinary shape where no auto-delegation is configured.
panels.title: Events routed and delegations started

panels.description: p95 by stage. `route.event` is the whole pass; the rest are its children — inline close checks, task_rule matching, team routing, the task upsert, trigger predicates, and the spawn enqueue. Read with the queue wait to the left, this says which half is slow: a short wait with a slow stage is slow routing, a long wait with fast stages is a backed-up queue. A stage with no calls in the window is absent rather than drawn at zero.
panels.title: Routing stage latency (p95)

panels.description: One row per trigger firing that waited on the firing queue, most recent first: a delegation decided while its task was busy, or one a score re-evaluation admitted, fired by the firing worker once the task is free. `Duration` is the worker's pass over the row (the live checks and the fenced run insert), not the time the row waited. A row with no `outcome` and `status` `unset` fired; open it for the `blueprint_run.id` it started, which its `route.delegate` child carries too. `task_busy` and `skipped_<reason>` are anticipated: another run went live first and the row waits again, or the row retired without firing because the task or trigger changed while it waited (`skipped_task_closed`, `skipped_claim_changed`, `skipped_trigger_disabled`, `skipped_breaker_tripped`, `skipped_already_fired`). `lease_lost` is the row passing to another holder and `cancelled` someone cancelling it through the work-queue API; neither is a failure. A failure has `status` `error` and no `outcome`, and the row is tried again. Empty means no firing waited in the window.
panels.title: Deferred firings

panels.description: One row per evaluation of a task's deferred triggers (those gated on a minimum autonomy suitability) after its score was written, most recent first. Every scoring pass queues one for each task it scored, and score writes that land while a task's row waits fold into that row. `Duration` is the evaluation and the transaction that admits its firings. `rederive.planned_firings` is how many firings the new score earned; each is admitted to the firing queue unless one for the same trigger is already waiting there, so the count can exceed the new Deferred firings rows, and most rows are `completed` with 0. `score_moved` means a newer score landed mid-evaluation, so nothing was admitted and the row was deferred to the newer score. `score_moved`, `lease_lost` and `cancelled` are anticipated, not failures; a failure has `status` `error`, and the row is tried again. Empty means nothing was scored in the window.
panels.title: Score re-evaluations

panels.description: One `engagement.setup` root per claim attempt, from the claim to agent-live. What follows agent-live is punctual spans linked back to it rather than children, because a span exports only once it ends and the streaming period is unbounded. Local mode takes a shorter path — no broker, sidecar, or credential spans exist there at all — and their absence is the path not taken, never a fault.
panels.title: Delegated runs — engagement setup

panels.description: One row per claim attempt, most recent first; `Duration` is the whole setup, claim to agent-live. `outcome` is the closed set — `agent_live` reached the agent, `cancelled` was stopped by someone, `shutdown` stood down for its departing executor and left the claim for the boot reconcile, `fenced` lost the conversation to a successor, `no_message` had nothing to deliver, `not_started` is an exit that did not say why, and `setup_failed` is the only one that also carries an error status. An error rate over engagements therefore has to read this attribute rather than the span status, or every stopped run counts as a failure. A requeued run is one row per attempt, sharing `conversation.id` and told apart by `claim.attempt`. Click a Span ID for the setup waterfall; empty means nothing was claimed in the window.
panels.title: Engagement setups — outcome and attempt

panels.description: Mean wall clock per call for each setup phase: the fleet-level answer to "why did that run take four minutes to start". For one specific run, open its trace from the table to the left instead. The phases NEST — `engagement.sandbox.bringup` contains the `sandbox.*` and `sidecar.*` children — so the lines deliberately do not stack and do not sum to the root. The credential park that also sits inside bring-up has its own panel below, since it measures another pod's work rather than this one's. In local mode the sandbox, sidecar and jail phases have no calls and are simply absent, leaving fetch, clone, staging and the SDK install.
panels.title: Setup phase breakdown — mean duration

panels.description: p95 of the two halves of credential provisioning, which are two traces on purpose: `engagement.credentials.await` is the executor parked in `awaiting_credentials`, `credentials.provision` is the control pod sealing a bundle to that run's sidecar key. They are deliberately not linked — the doorbell between them is lossy by design and the sweep is the real completion path, so a link would promise a handoff neither side can guarantee. Both carry `conversation.id`, which is the join for one run: search it in Explore. A park much longer than the seal means the doorbell was missed and the sweep collected it; the `count` attribute on the await span is the poll count that says which. Both are empty in local mode, which has no sidecar to seal to.
panels.title: Credential wait — the park and the seal

panels.description: One row per privileged host operation the executor asked the cap-broker to perform, slowest first; `Duration` is the round trip as the caller experienced it. The broker exports no spans of its own — permanently, so the most privileged process on the host gains no outbound network dependency — which makes these client-side spans the only record its work has anywhere. `op` is the broker method, a Go constant from the dispatching switch: filter it to compare `SetupNetwork` against `LaunchRun` against a teardown. Teardown calls land in their run's trace after the setup root ended, so a trace legitimately reads setup, gap, tail. Empty in local mode: there is no broker there.
panels.title: Broker IPC calls by op

panels.description: The spans that cover a run after setup ends. None is a child of the `engagement.setup` root, which ends at agent-live: a span exports only once it ends, so one held open across the run would be lost with it on a crash. Each starts a short trace of its own, except a sandboxed run's `commit_signing.sign`, which sits inside the `relay.call` that carried it. Most link back to the run's setup trace, and every one carries `conversation.id`: search it in Explore for everything one run did after setup.
panels.title: Delegated runs — after agent-live

panels.description: One row per result a run's agent handed back, most recent first: the moment an engagement ended and TF recorded what it came to. `runtime` is `sdk` or `native`; every delegated run on a multi-mode deployment is `native`. The span's own `Duration` is that bookkeeping (recording the result, snapshotting the workspace), not the run; the run's figures are the attributes: `agent.cost_usd`, `agent.duration_ms` (the agent's own wall clock), and `turns`. On a `native` row `agent.cost_usd` is what that one engagement's model calls cost, compaction calls included. `outcome`: `concluded_<verdict>` returned a verdict; `open` parked with no conclusion, waiting on a next message (on `native` also a stop, or a guard that parked the run); `invalid_envelope` (`sdk` only) gave a conclusion that never validated; `failed_<kind>` ended the run as failed, `failed_agent_error` being the runtime reporting an error; `fenced` was dropped because the claim had been released or its lease had lapsed, and the conversation's next claim concludes it. Three are `native` only, and each hands the claim back with the conversation mid-flight: `shutdown` (the executor stopped), `upstream_unavailable` (the model provider stayed unavailable through the retries, or went silent), and `jail_lost` (the sandbox died and could not be restarted in place). A run that fails before it has a result to hand back (a setup failure, or an `sdk` run's resume or stream failure) has no row here; the conversation records that failure.

targets.query: { name = "engagement.complete" } | select(span.outcome, span.runtime, span.agent.cost_usd, span.agent.duration_ms, span.count, span.conversation.id)

panels.title: Run completions

panels.description: One row per op a sandboxed run's sidecar relayed to its executor, most recent first: the agent's `tfac exec` verbs, and the sidecar's own questions and audit records for what the agent did through its proxies (a push to authorize, a `gh` write to record, a commit digest to sign). `relay.call` is a request the sidecar waits on; `relay.record` applies the audit record of an external write that already happened. `op` is `<namespace>.<op>`, both halves Go constants: `core.*` for TF's own ops, a provider's namespace (`slack.*`) for its verbs. `Duration` is the executor's half of one op. `status` `error` on a `relay.call` is an op that failed; on a `relay.record` it is a record that did not apply, either lost (the Audit pipeline row counts it) or deferred, in which case the sidecar sends it again. Empty in local mode, where verbs reach TF without a sidecar.
panels.title: Agent exec verbs

panels.description: One row per tool-permission prompt a run raised, most recent first. `Duration` is the time the run waited on a person, the one stretch a run's own accounting leaves out, so nothing else TF records shows it. `outcome`: `answered_allow` or `answered_deny` is a person deciding; `timeout` is the whole window running out; `absent` is the early deny for a prompt nobody was watching. The tool's name is deliberately not recorded. Fills only from local mode: native runs never prompt, so the bundled multi stack leaves it empty.
panels.title: Permission prompts — the human wait

panels.description: One row per repository check and per recorded push, most recent first, in both modes. `git.authorize` is the managed Git proxy checking that the run may reach a repository. It runs on every git request the agent sends through the proxy, so a clone, fetch or push makes two or more rows (the ref advertisement, then each pack request). The request waits on it, so its `Duration` is time that git command stalled. `outcome` is `allowed` or `denied_<reason>` (`denied_repo-not-tracked`, `denied_repo-not-materialized`); `status` `error` is a check that could not be made, and the proxy refuses the request. `git.record_push` writes a push to the audit log and carries no `outcome`: it says the record arrived and how long the write took, and the store spans under it say whether it landed. The repository is deliberately not recorded.
panels.title: Git proxy gate

panels.description: One row per commit signature asked for or decided, most recent first. `commit_signing.sign` is the run's side, and `mode` says where the signature was made: `local` in the TF process for a local run, `control_plane` for a sandboxed run, whose `Duration` includes the wait for a control pod's answer. `commit_signing.decide` is that control pod deciding, in a trace of its own and with no `mode`. `signer` is the kind of signer, `org` or `deployment`. `outcome` is `signed`; `refused`, with `reason` saying why; or `unanswered`, no answer reached the run in time and it is told to try again. A decide row records a request it could not answer as `refused` with `reason` `unanswered`. The other reasons: `claim_budget` and `org_minute_budget` are the signing budgets; `signer_changed`, `signer_removed`, `signer_inactive` and `not_signing` are the signer; `claim_inactive` is an engagement that no longer holds its claim; `committer_mismatch` is a commit whose committer is not the run's signer; `not_a_commit` is a tag or push certificate. `status` `error` is a request or decision that could not be made or stored. Empty when the org signs no commits.

targets.query: { name =~ "commit_signing\\.(sign|decide)" } | select(span.outcome, status, span.signer, span.mode, span.reason, span.conversation.id)

panels.title: Commit signing

panels.description: Every park and every non-failed terminal writes the run's workspace to the blob store, and the status flip that follows is serialized behind that write — so a stop that sat in WORKING for a minute is answerable here. One punctual `workspace.snapshot` trace per snapshot, linked back to its engagement, with three children naming where the time went: `capture` (the git delta + transcript read), `archive` (the tar walk + gzip), `put` (the blob write). Coverage is both modes — tracing is gated solely on TF_TRACES_ENDPOINT, and local mode emits this family in full. The capture phase is the one that differs by mode: local runs it in-process, multi routes it through the privileged capture child, which is span-free by standing decision — the executor-side `capture` span IS its measurement. `runtime` rides on every span because the members are not runtime-agnostic: only a delegated SDK run snapshots a session transcript, so transcript sizes are SDK-run data, never a property of all snapshots.
panels.title: Workspace snapshots — the park and the terminal

panels.description: One row per snapshot, most recent first; `Duration` is the whole write — and the lower bound on how long the run's status flip waited behind it. `size_bytes` is the compressed blob as stored, the parked-window storage cost. A slow row's phase split is one click away: open the Span ID for the waterfall. Empty means nothing parked or concluded in the window.
panels.title: Workspace snapshots — duration and footprint

panels.description: Mean wall clock per phase, fleet-wide: which of the three costs a slow snapshot is actually paying. `capture` is the git bundle/diff plus the transcript read (in multi mode, the whole privileged capture child, timed from the executor side); `archive` is the tar walk plus gzip; `put` is the blob upload. The phases are sequential and sum to roughly the parent — unlike the setup phases, nothing here nests.
panels.title: Snapshot phase breakdown — mean duration

panels.description: What the capture phase read, per snapshot: the git bundle (committed work), the uncommitted patch, and the session transcript. `transcript_bytes` is populated only where `runtime` is `sdk` — native conversations never snapshot a transcript, so a zero on a native row is the member not existing, not a failed read. A non-git run-root (a Jira lazy run) reports zero bundle and patch the same way.
panels.title: Capture members — bundle, patch, transcript

panels.description: The archive phase's report card: `snapshot.raw_bytes` went into the compressor, `size_bytes` came out as the stored blob. Ratio from the pair, throughput from either against the row's duration — which is exactly the before/after a codec change has to prove itself against, from the field rather than a benchmark.
panels.title: Archive compression — raw in, gzipped out

panels.description: Audit records that never reached the log of record. Every external write an agent makes is applied upstream before TF records it, so a failure to record it may never unwind the act. TF retries instead: the database write is retried on a retryable error, and a sandboxed run's sidecar resends each record until the orchestrator acknowledges it. What is still lost — at the sidecar's send, the orchestrator's decode, a provider handler's own dispatch, or the database write — is counted here. Flat zero is the expected shape, and the only interesting one: a single drop is a hole in the log, not a blip to smooth over. One residual is outside what this can see — records held by a sidecar that dies before its cell is torn down go with it, and so does the report of their loss.
panels.title: Audit pipeline — records that never landed

panels.description: Audit records lost over the dashboard's time range, summed across every pod and stage. The number to look at first, and the number that should be 0. Anything else means the external_actions table is missing rows for writes that really happened — read the two panels beside this one for which stage lost them and what they were, then the pod's WARN lines, which name the target this deliberately does not.
panels.title: Audit records dropped

panels.description: Where in the funnel each record was lost. `record` is the database write and is the only stage a local-mode deployment can reach — there is no sidecar and no relay there, so the other three staying empty is the path not taken, not a gap. `relay_send` is the sidecar reporting, at the end of the run, records the orchestrator never applied; `relay_decode` is a payload that arrived and could not be turned back into a record; `relay_dispatch` is a provider's own record handler failing. A record is counted at the stage that finally lost it, never at two; the `record` stage counts each row it lost, so a record whose artifact and action both failed counts twice there.
panels.title: Drops by stage

panels.description: What was being recorded when it was lost, over the dashboard's time range. `op` is read in the vocabulary of its stage: a `<namespace>.<op>` relay pair for the relay stages (`core.record_gh_write`, `slack.record_thread_root`, …), the row's own domain kind (`pull_request`, `gh_channel_write`, `pr_merged`) for the database write. `other` is a name that arrived on the wire matching no op this binary serves — the label is clamped against the registered ops on purpose, since the sending process is the one exposed to hostile text and an unclamped label would be an unbounded series. Nothing here names a repository, a target, or an id; the pod's WARN line does.
panels.title: Drops by op

panels.description: Requests TF makes to GitHub, Jira, Slack's Web API, and the LLM providers, by how each one ended, and the connection state each org's poll cycles record for GitHub and Jira. Scraped from each pod's :9464 and summed across pods; tf_upstream_up is exported by the pod holding the background brain only. Every org brings its own upstream, so one org failing is usually that org's own GitHub Enterprise Server, Jira Data Center, or credential; many orgs failing against the same upstream at once is the fleet-wide case the UpstreamFailingFleetWide and UpstreamDownFleetWide rules alert on. `org_id` is the org a request was made for, and is empty for a request made for no org. The two wait panels at the bottom of the row are built from traces instead, so they are empty with tracing off.
panels.title: Connections — upstream systems

panels.description: One count per HTTP attempt, so a call retried twice adds three. `rate_limited`: the upstream asked TF to wait (a 429, or one of GitHub's rate-limit 403s). `transient`: a 5xx, a 408, a transport failure, or a 403 whose body is not a JSON object, which comes from a proxy in front of the upstream rather than the upstream itself. `auth`: a 401, or a JSON 403 that is not a rate limit. `rejected`: any other 4xx, meaning the request itself was wrong.
panels.title: Requests by outcome

panels.description: Decisions to retry, by the outcome of the attempt that caused the retry. GitHub retries a GET or a GraphQL query after a rate limit or a transient failure, and never a mutation; Jira retries a 429 on any call, and a transient failure on an idempotent one; neither retries a non-JSON 403, a TLS failure, or a timeout, which another attempt would only repeat; Slack retries one 429 whose Retry-After is 30s or less. A mutation that fails transiently is not retried, so it shows in Requests by outcome and not here. A retry that then succeeds counts here once, and its successful attempt counts as `ok` in Requests by outcome.
panels.title: Retries

panels.description: Per upstream, the number of orgs for which more than half of the attempts in the last 5 minutes ended `transient` or `auth`: the numerator of the UpstreamFailingFleetWide rule in docker/observability/rules/tf-connections.yml, over the same window. Requests made for no org are not counted. No data means no org is failing.

targets.expr: count by (upstream) ((sum by (upstream, org_id) (rate(tf_upstream_requests_total{org_id!="",outcome=~"transient|auth"}[5m])) / sum by (upstream, org_id) (rate(tf_upstream_requests_total{org_id!=""}[5m]))) > 0.5)

panels.title: Orgs with failing requests

panels.description: Per upstream, the number of orgs whose last GitHub or Jira poll cycle that made requests got no answer: every request failed in transit, or was refused for its credential (tf_upstream_up 0). The numerator of the UpstreamDownFleetWide rule in docker/observability/rules/tf-connections.yml. A cycle that met only rate limits leaves an org's state where it was; one that skipped the source on purpose (turned off, no credential, nothing tracked) clears it, and the org drops out. 0 means no org is down; no data means no org has a recorded state.
panels.title: Orgs down by upstream

panels.description: Every org whose stored GitHub or Jira connection state is down right now, and the upstream it is down against. The pod's log says when each went down and why: one WARN `<source> connection lost` with the org and the failure class (`transient` or `auth`), then one INFO `<source> connection restored` with `down_for` when it comes back, or one INFO `<source> connection no longer checked` when the poller stops checking it.
panels.title: Orgs down

panels.description: Per org, the conversations a hand-back is holding out of the queue until a time: the model provider was unavailable through an engagement's own retries, or GitHub could not be reached while it set up its workspace, so the engagement handed its claim back to be tried again on a backoff (30s, 1m, 2m, 5m, then every 10m) instead of failing the run (tf_conversations_deferred). They display as queued but count toward no queue depth, age or position. A person's message retries one at once. After about four hours of attempts a conversation parks as upstream_unavailable and leaves this count. The ConversationsDeferred rule in docker/observability/rules/tf-connections.yml warns when the total stays above zero for 30 minutes. No data means no org has a deferred conversation.
panels.title: Conversations waiting to retry

panels.description: Claims given back with the conversation still mid-flight, so the next claim continues it, by why (tf_conversations_handed_back_total, summed across executors). requeued: the engagement failed before its agent ran, and counts toward the setup budget. requeued_credentials: the credential bundle never arrived. requeued_shutdown: the executor stopped or drained. requeued_upstream: the model provider stayed unavailable through the engagement's retries or went silent, or GitHub could not be reached during workspace setup, and the conversation waits on a backoff before its next claim. requeued_jail_lost: the sandbox a native run's tools ran in died and could not be restarted in place, and counts toward the jail budget. A lease takeover (reaped) is not counted here; see tf_claims_expired.
panels.title: Hand-backs by outcome

panels.description: Seconds spent asleep per second, deployment-wide, by kind of wait. `github.ratelimit.await` is a GitHub call held back because its rate-limit budget is spent; `github.ratelimit.backoff` and `jira.retry.backoff` are the wait before a retry. These are inline waits of up to five minutes for GitHub and 30 seconds for Jira, and without them a call waiting out a limit looks identical to slow HTTP. A value of 1 is, on average, one call asleep at every moment. A wait counts once it ends. GitHub and Jira only: Linear and Slack start no span for a wait, and their rate-limit waits are counted, with GitHub's and Jira's, in tf_upstream_rate_limit_wait_seconds_total. For one wait and the call it held up, use the table beside this one.
panels.title: Time spent waiting on upstream limits

panels.description: One row per wait, most recent first; `Duration` is the time spent asleep. `github.ratelimit.await` holds a GitHub call until its spent budget resets: `waited`, or `refused` when the reset is more than five minutes off and the call fails as rate-limited instead. `github.ratelimit.backoff` and `jira.retry.backoff` are the wait before a retry: `attempt` is the attempt that failed, so 3 is a call's third wait, and `disposition` is why, `rate_limited` or `transient` for GitHub and `throttled` or `transport_error` for Jira. `cancelled` on any of them is the caller leaving mid-wait. None of these is an error status. Open a row for the call or poll cycle the wait sat inside. GitHub and Jira only: Linear and Slack start no span for a wait. Empty is the healthy state.
